lead: A superheterodyne receiver (superhet) shifts every station it tunes to one fixed intermediate frequency (IF), 455 kHz in AM broadcast radios, and does most of its amplifying and filtering there. Fixed-frequency stages are easy to make with high gain and a sharp, flat passband, which tuned stages that must sweep a whole band are not. The shift is done by a mixer fed from a local oscillator (LO) that is tuned together with the input. The cost is the image: a second input frequency that the mixer also turns into the IF, and that only the tuned stages before the mixer can reject.
prereq: You need: mixing as multiplication (sum and difference frequencies), as in AM generation: square-law and balanced modulators, and the envelope detector of AM demodulation: envelope and coherent detectors.

sections.h3: The blocks and what each one does

items: RF stage: a tuned circuit, often with an amplifier, selects the wanted signal fs, rejects the image and improves the noise figure.
Mixer and local oscillator: the mixer multiplies fs by fLO and its output tank keeps the difference fLO − fs = fIF.
IF amplifier: two or three fixed tuned stages, or a ceramic filter, give most of the gain and set the selectivity (about 10 kHz wide for AM broadcast).
Detector: an envelope detector recovers the audio and a DC level proportional to the carrier.
AGC: automatic gain control filters that DC level and feeds it back to cut the RF and IF gain on strong stations, so loud and weak stations come out at similar volume.

blocks.text: Receivers are judged on four properties. Sensitivity is the weakest signal that gives a standard output. Selectivity is the ability to reject a neighbouring channel; the IF stage sets it. Fidelity is how faithfully the audio band is reproduced. Image rejection is the subject of the next section. The figure draws the chain with the frequencies of the worked example.

sections.h3: The local oscillator, the image and image rejection

blocks.text: Most broadcast receivers use high-side injection: the LO runs above the signal.
for high-side injection: f<sub>s</sub> is the wanted signal, f<sub>LO</sub> the local oscillator and f<sub>si</sub> the image, all in hertz.

The image f<sub>si</sub> lies f<sub>IF</sub> above the LO, so it too gives f<sub>si</sub> − f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>IF</sub> at the mixer output. Once both are at 455 kHz nothing can separate them; the rejection must happen in the tuned RF stages, which are tuned to f<sub>s</sub> and see the image 2f<sub>IF</sub> away. With low-side injection f<sub>LO</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>IF</sub> and the image is f<sub>s</sub> − 2f<sub>IF</sub>.
A single tuned circuit of loaded quality factor Q, tuned to f<sub>s</sub>, passes the image weaker than the signal by the image-rejection ratio α:
α is a voltage ratio (20 log α in dB); ρ is the fractional detuning of the image. Two tuned stages multiply: α = α<sub>1</sub>α<sub>2</sub>.

For a fixed IF, ρ shrinks as f<sub>s</sub> rises, because the image is a smaller fraction away. A shortwave receiver with a 455 kHz IF therefore rejects images poorly, as the worked example shows. The cure is a higher IF, or double conversion: a high first IF (several megahertz) to push the image far away, then a low second IF for selectivity.

sections.h3: Tracking, choice of IF and double spotting

blocks.text: One knob tunes the RF circuit and the LO together on a ganged capacitor, keeping f<sub>LO</sub> − f<sub>s</sub> = f<sub>IF</sub> across the band. This is tracking. For 540 to 1650 kHz the RF circuit spans a frequency ratio of 3.06, which needs a capacitance ratio of 3.06² = 9.34. The LO spans 995 to 2105 kHz, a ratio of only 2.12 (capacitance ratio 4.48). The LO section therefore has a series padder capacitor and a parallel trimmer, and the error is made zero at three points of the band (three-point tracking). Low-side injection would need the LO to span 85 to 1195 kHz, a ratio of 14, which a variable capacitor cannot cover: one reason for high-side injection.

Choosing the IF is a compromise. A high IF puts the image far away (good image rejection) and eases tracking. A low IF gives narrow, steep IF filters (good selectivity) and more stable gain. The IF must not fall inside the tuning band, or a strong station there would pass straight through. Double spotting, hearing a strong station at two dial settings 2f<sub>IF</sub> apart, is the image problem seen from the dial and points to a weak RF stage.

examples.question: A broadcast superhet with a 455 kHz IF and high-side injection is tuned to 1000 kHz. Its RF stage is one tuned circuit with Q = 100. Find f<sub>LO</sub>, the image and the image rejection. Repeat for a shortwave signal at 25 MHz with the same IF and Q, and with a 1.5 MHz IF.
steps: Two identical tuned stages at 1000 kHz would give 138.6² = 19 223, or 85.7 dB.
examples.answer: f<sub>LO</sub> = 1455 kHz, f<sub>si</sub> = 1910 kHz, α = 138.6 (42.8 dB). At 25 MHz: 7.22 (17.2 dB) with a 455 kHz IF, 22.7 (27.1 dB) with a 1.5 MHz IF.

traps: Writing f<sub>si</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> + 2f<sub>IF</sub> for low-side injection. It holds only when the LO is above the signal; with the LO below, f<sub>si</sub> = f<sub>s</sub> − 2f<sub>IF</sub>.
Saying the IF filter rejects the image. After the mixer the image is already at the IF; only the RF stages can reject it.
Using ρ = (f<sub>si</sub> − f<sub>s</sub>)/f<sub>s</sub>. The formula is ρ = f<sub>si</sub>/f<sub>s</sub> − f<sub>s</sub>/f<sub>si</sub>: 1.3864, not 0.91, at 1000 kHz.
Adding the dB of two stages wrongly: multiply the ratios (138.6 × 138.6), or add the dB (42.8 + 42.8 = 85.7 dB).

quiz.q: Define sensitivity, selectivity and fidelity of a receiver.
quiz.a: Sensitivity: the weakest input that gives a standard output. Selectivity: the ability to reject adjacent channels. Fidelity: how evenly the audio band is reproduced.

quiz.q: A receiver with f<sub>IF</sub> = 455 kHz and high-side injection is tuned to 800 kHz. Find f<sub>LO</sub> and the image.
A high-side receiver has f<sub>LO</sub> = 1500 kHz and f<sub>IF</sub> = 455 kHz. Find the tuned station and its image.
Find the image rejection at 600 kHz for f<sub>IF</sub> = 455 kHz and Q = 80.
Why does a fixed 455 kHz IF give poor image rejection at shortwave?
quiz.a: The image is 910 kHz away whatever the signal, which is a small fraction of 25 MHz, so ρ is small (0.0715) and one tuned circuit gives only α = 7.22.

quiz.q: What is double spotting, and what does it show?
quiz.a: Hearing a strong station at two dial points 2f<sub>IF</sub> apart, once as the wanted signal and once as an image. It shows weak RF selectivity.

quiz.q: Explain why broadcast receivers use high-side injection, using the LO tuning range.
quiz.a: For 540 to 1650 kHz the high-side LO spans 995 to 2105 kHz, a 2.12 ratio (capacitance 4.48). A low-side LO would span 85 to 1195 kHz, a ratio of 14 (capacitance about 198), beyond any ganged capacitor.

beyond: Phones and Wi-Fi chips mostly use zero-IF or low-IF receivers, which mix straight to baseband with an I/Q mixer and cancel the image by phase instead of by an RF filter. Software-defined radios sample a wide band at once and do the IF filtering in software. Search next for image-reject mixer, zero-IF receiver and direct-sampling SDR.

Below, a frequency axis from 800 to 2000 kHz with the signal at 1000, LO at 1455 and image at 1910 kHz, 455 kHz apart, under the narrow tuning curve of the RF stage.
